title: Repeated drug exposure recruits ΔFosB in defined neurons
body: **ΔFosB** is a shortened protein produced from an alternatively spliced transcript of the FosB gene. It acts as a **transcription factor**, a protein that regulates the expression of other genes. Repeated stimulation can therefore change how a neuron responds long after an individual drug exposure. Lobo and colleagues measured ΔFosB in identified mouse striatal neurons after repeated drug treatment. Their cell labeling separated two neuronal populations that would be mixed together in a whole-tissue measurement.

**Medium spiny neurons** are inhibitory projection neurons named for the small protrusions on their dendrites. The **nucleus accumbens**, a ventral part of the striatum, contains core and shell subdivisions. The investigators distinguished neurons expressing D1-type dopamine receptors from those expressing D2-type receptors. Seven daily cocaine treatments increased ΔFosB predominantly in D1-type neurons in the examined striatal regions. The response was measured 24 h after the final treatment, separating persistent protein induction from the immediate drug exposure.

Different substances recruited different cell populations in the same study. Voluntary cocaine self-administration also favored ΔFosB induction in D1-type neurons. Morphine treatment and heroin self-administration recruited both D1-type and D2-type populations. Sucrose exposure and environmental enrichment could also increase ΔFosB in both populations. The relationship between repeated experience and gene regulation therefore depends on the substance, the neuronal population and the conditions of exposure.

title: Phosphorylation helps ΔFosB resist degradation
body: **Protein half-life** is the time over which half of a labeled protein population disappears. Ulery and colleagues measured ΔFosB turnover using a pulse of labeled amino acids followed by an unlabeled chase. In PC12 cells, a rat-derived neuron-like preparation, ΔFosB had a half-life of approximately 10 h. Full-length FosB was already known to turn over much faster in cell culture. These measurements concern protein persistence within the preparation, rather than the duration of an animal’s behavioral response.

**Phosphorylation** adds a phosphate group to a protein and can change its interactions or stability. The investigators identified serine at position 27, termed **Ser27**, as a stabilizing phosphorylation site. Replacing this serine with alanine prevented phosphorylation at that position. In PC12 cells, this substitution shortened the measured half-life from approximately 11 h to approximately 4 h. A substitution that partly mimicked the phosphate’s negative charge instead increased protein stability.

A **proteasome** is a cellular complex that breaks down selected proteins. Two different proteasome inhibitors reversed the accelerated loss of the alanine-substituted ΔFosB protein. This result connects the altered amino acid to a specific route of protein degradation. The study also identified **casein kinase 2**, an enzyme that transfers phosphate groups, as a regulator of Ser27 phosphorylation. Protein stabilization supplies a molecular mechanism through which repeated activation can sustain a transcriptional response after the initiating stimulus has ended.

figure.caption: Ulery et al. (2006), Fig. 6. Ser27 substitutions change ΔFosB protein turnover.

title: ΔFosB and CaMKII couple gene regulation to plasticity
body: **CaMKII** is calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II, an enzyme whose activation links calcium signals to protein phosphorylation. Robison and colleagues examined its relationship with ΔFosB in the nucleus accumbens. Repeated cocaine exposure in rats increased CaMKII particularly in the accumbens shell under the tested conditions. ΔFosB promoted expression of the gene encoding the alpha form of CaMKII in D1-type neurons. This transcriptional relationship connects a persistent nuclear protein with a signaling enzyme that acts within neurons.

The investigators manipulated ΔFosB using viral expression in mouse accumbens neurons. Increasing ΔFosB increased the density of **dendritic spines**, small neuronal protrusions that receive many excitatory synaptic contacts. Coexpressing a peptide inhibitor of CaMKII prevented this structural effect. The same manipulation also prevented the enhanced locomotor response to cocaine associated with ΔFosB expression. These interventions connect the molecular pathway to both neuronal structure and a measured drug-related behavior.

CaMKII also phosphorylated ΔFosB at Ser27, linking the kinase back to the transcription factor’s stability. The two proteins consequently participated in a positive regulatory loop in the tested accumbens preparation. **Sensitization** refers here to an increased behavioral response following repeated drug exposure. The study measured this response through cocaine-induced locomotion and examined it alongside molecular and structural changes. Cell identity and accumbens subregion determine where this particular loop is engaged.

Behavioral and structural responses to chronic cocaine require a feedforward loop involving ΔFosB and calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II in the nucleus accumbens shell. title: Social stress recruits different ΔFosB cell populations
body: Lobo and colleagues exposed mice to 10 d of repeated social defeat and then measured their social interaction. **Susceptible** animals displayed reduced interaction under the study’s behavioral classification. **Resilient** animals maintained social interaction despite exposure to the same defeat procedure. The researchers then measured ΔFosB separately in D1-type and D2-type medium spiny neurons. This approach retained information about which cells responded, rather than averaging the two populations together.

Susceptible mice had increased ΔFosB in D2-type neurons in accumbens core, accumbens shell and dorsal striatum. Resilient mice instead had increased ΔFosB in D1-type neurons in those regions. These measurements were obtained after the defeat episodes and social-interaction assessment. Opposite behavioral outcomes were therefore associated with induction in different neuronal populations. A rise in total ΔFosB alone would omit the cell-type distinction that separated the two outcomes.

The study also examined repeated treatment with **fluoxetine**, an antidepressant that inhibits serotonin reuptake. Fourteen days of treatment increased ΔFosB predominantly in D1-type neurons in the examined striatal regions. Cocaine exposure, social resilience and antidepressant treatment could consequently share a cell-type pattern while occurring under different experimental conditions. ΔFosB is part of experience-dependent gene regulation across rewarding, stressful and pharmacological contexts. The behavioral meaning of its induction depends on the cells and the experience that recruited it.

title: Human ΔFosB findings depend on the sampled brain region
body: Human research has examined ΔFosB in postmortem tissue from people with cocaine dependence and comparison subjects. Robison and colleagues found increased ΔFosB and CaMKII in the sampled human nucleus accumbens. Their rodent experiments supplied interventions that linked these proteins to cocaine-responsive cellular and behavioral changes. The human measurements established a corresponding molecular association in a clinically relevant brain region. Postmortem comparisons alone leave the timing of the molecular change relative to drug use unresolved.

Gajewski and colleagues examined two additional regions: the **hippocampus**, involved in memory processing, and the **prefrontal cortex**, involved in the regulation of behavior. They separated FosB-family proteins by molecular mass using a **Western blot**, an antibody-based protein assay. Cocaine-dependent subjects had lower hippocampal ΔFosB and several other FosB-family signals than comparison subjects. The sampled prefrontal cortex did not exhibit the same group differences. The direction of a human molecular finding therefore changes with the region being examined.

The hippocampal samples also had reduced **GluA2**, a subunit of AMPA-type receptors that carry excitatory glutamate signals. This finding accompanied the altered FosB-family protein pattern in that region. Human and mouse samples shared major FosB-family protein bands, while human tissue contained additional detected bands. The authors used mouse tissue controls to investigate whether delayed collection could explain those additional signals. Across these studies, regional sampling and protein identification determine how animal mechanisms can be compared with human molecular observations.
